mechanisms: Financial capacity and secure collateral determine feasibility, because low income and insecure land tenure make high-cost investments unattainable without subsidy.
Knowledge and openness to innovation shape evaluation, because higher education, youth, or awareness of benefits make new practices seem viable and attractive.
Perceived risk and incompatibility with traditional methods dominate, because poor connectivity, digital illiteracy, or mistrust make digital tools feel unreliable and alien.
Management complexity and uncertainty increase, because lack of access to training, extension, or timely inputs leaves farmers feeling incapable of implementing new practices.
Attachment to customary grazing and scepticism of external interventions prevail, because embeddedness in traditional cultural norms or social inequality makes unfamiliar practices suspect.
objection_patterns: Can I afford the upfront and running costs without a subsidy?
Will this work with my current farming methods and traditions?
Do I trust the people and institutions behind this?
Will I get the training and timely support needed to make this work?
confidence: Mixed-methods and review, multiple South African provinces, fieldwork 2018-2020 — mechanisms durable, magnitudes unknown.
